headline: U.S. Growth Revision Does Not Close the PCE Policy Case
deck: October prices rose from a year earlier as stronger third-quarter activity was revised into the record.
body: BEA’s second estimate put U.S. real gross domestic product growth at a 4.3% annual rate in the third quarter, after 2.2% in the second quarter. The agency said the estimate was revised up 0.9 percentage point from the advance release, chiefly because investment and consumer spending were revised higher; Axios said the advance estimate had been 3.4%. [E6] [E8] [E11]

October’s PCE price index rose 0.3% from September, with the core measure excluding food and energy also up 0.3%. The headline index was 3.8% higher than a year earlier and core PCE was 3.3% higher; AP reported that the 3.8% annual reading was up from 3.6% in September. [E4] [E5] [E9]

Household spending supplies a useful bridge between the two releases, but it is not one number. Personal outlays rose $69.3 billion in October and the saving rate was 4.1%; current-dollar PCE rose $63.8 billion, led by $52.1 billion more spending on services, while real PCE fell $5.8 billion, less than 0.1% at a monthly rate. [E1] [E2] [E3]
Investment, consumer spending and government spending contributed to third-quarter real GDP growth, while exports fell and imports increased. [E7]
AP reported that many Federal Reserve officials had signalled support for raising the short-term rate and that economists expected an increase at the 8–9 December policy meeting. [E10]

**The desk's reading.** The upward revision makes the third-quarter activity picture stronger, and the October price readings keep the inflation problem live. The strongest contrary reading is that the combination already points cleanly to tighter policy. It does not: one release is a revised, annualized account of July through September, while the other is a price reading for October; neither one alone states how officials will weigh the other data before their meeting.

**The next test.** The Federal Reserve’s 8–9 December decision and accompanying statement will separate the readings. A rate increase framed around persistent price pressure would strengthen the case that October dominated the judgment; a hold that stresses uncertainty or other incoming evidence would show that the two releases did not settle it.
